No. The story stays tightly within Ilse's point of view. The other characters (Kalle, the boy, Frau Mertens) are vivid but seen only from the outside, through brief gestures and dialogue.

The one figure who might be unlikeable is Jonas, who sends the care-home brochure with only a yellow sticky note and calls at odd hours about the house. He is presented solely through Ilse's guesses about what he wants. His own motives and worries are never voiced, so his perspective isn't conveyed at all, let alone convincingly.

Ilse herself is somewhat ambiguous in choosing not to answer her son's call, and her mindset is rendered believably. Still, the story offers essentially one perspective rather than diverse ones.
